title: Can You Get PIP for Arthritis? UK Points & Evidence
meta_title: Does Arthritis Qualify for PIP? Eligibility & Evidence
meta_description: PIP eligibility for arthritis: awards depend on how daily living and mobility are affected, not the diagnosis. Points, evidence and how decisions are made.
excerpt: Can you claim PIP for arthritis while working? Learn how daily living, mobility and fluctuating symptoms are assessed, and what evidence to prepare.
direct_answer: Arthritis can affect a PIP claim, but the diagnosis alone does not qualify you. Awards depend on assessed daily living and mobility activities, reliability and how often difficulties occur, alongside other eligibility rules. Check the correct national service: Scotland uses Adult Disability Payment for new working-age claims. You can receive PIP while working or with savings.

content:
Arthritis can turn an ordinary task into a difficult one: preparing a meal may take longer, fastening clothes may need help, or walking may require rests. For PIP, the important question is not simply which diagnosis you have. It is how your condition affects the assessed daily-living and mobility activities, whether you can do them reliably, and how often the difficulties occur. This guide explains those rules and how to describe your own experience honestly. First check the benefit and claim service for where you live; new working-age disability claims in Scotland use Adult Disability Payment.

This guide explains eligibility; our step-by-step claim guide covers the application process.

First check the benefit for where you live

  • England and Wales: use GOV.UK PIP eligibility guidance and the DWP claim service.
  • Northern Ireland: PIP is administered separately. Use nidirect's PIP service, including its claim and challenge instructions.
  • Scotland: new working-age disability claims use Adult Disability Payment, not PIP. Do not assume the DWP application or appeal process applies.

New PIP claims are usually for people aged 16 to below State Pension age. If you are above that age, Attendance Allowance is usually the new-claim route in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; in Scotland, check Pension Age Disability Payment. Existing awards and recent previous awards can change the position. Do not stop an existing benefit or assume you must switch because of this summary. Residence, time abroad and immigration rules also apply, with exceptions: check your nation's official guidance or get welfare advice.

What else must be true?

PIP is for long-term difficulties with daily living or getting around. The usual required period is difficulties for at least three months and an expectation that they will continue for at least another nine months, as explained in the DWP assessment-process guide. GOV.UK's public eligibility page summarises this as difficulties expected to last at least 12 months from when they started. Special rules apply near the end of life; do not use the ordinary waiting-period summary in that situation.

You can receive PIP while working or with savings. Income and savings do not determine its amount. This is not a test of whether you can work, and you do not need to wait until you leave work to check eligibility. Other benefits can interact with PIP, so ask an adviser about your whole situation rather than assuming every payment is unaffected.

Which activities and points matter?

PIP has two separately scored parts. Daily living covers ten activities, including preparing food, eating and drinking, managing treatment, washing, toilet needs, dressing, communicating, reading, engaging with people and budgeting. Mobility covers planning and following journeys, and physically moving around.

The scoring rules for daily living and mobility set separate thresholds. For each part separately, 8 to 11 points gives the standard rate and 12 or more the enhanced rate, if the other entitlement conditions are met. Daily living points cannot be added to mobility points to reach a threshold. You may receive one part, both or neither. These are not points for having a particular diagnosis, taking a particular medicine or having an abnormal scan.

The DWP criteria guide gives the activity descriptions and descriptors: statements about the kind of help or difficulty involved. An aid or another person's help may matter, but using an object does not automatically earn points. Explain why it is needed for that activity and what happens without it.

Reliable means more than doing something once

The reliability test applies across the activities. Can you do the task:

  • Safely: without an unacceptable risk of harm during or after it?
  • To an acceptable standard: is the task actually completed adequately?
  • Repeatedly: as often as reasonably needed, including the effects on later tasks or the next day?
  • In a reasonable time: no more than twice as long as the maximum time a person without a relevant disability would normally take?

For example, say if preparing a meal leaves your hands too painful to repeat the task when another meal is needed. Describe the time, recovery, help and frequency, not just that cooking hurts. Help you need can count even when nobody is available to provide it; explain how you currently manage and any risks.

How to describe flares and better days honestly

GOV.UK says difficulties must occur on more than half the days over a 12-month period. The detailed rules consider each activity and can combine different scoring descriptors across days. It is not necessary for one identical difficulty to happen every day. A welfare adviser can help apply those rules where the pattern is complicated.

Do not describe your worst day as every day, or let one better day stand for the whole year. Record how many days are affected, which activities change, how long a flare lasts, and what remains difficult between flares. A printable PIP evidence diary can organise examples. A short diary supports your account; it is not itself the full required period or a reason to miss a form deadline.

Useful arthritis examples, without promising points

  • Preparing food: describe peeling, chopping and cooking a simple meal, the help or equipment needed and safety. The DWP activity does not include carrying shopping or carrying food around the kitchen.
  • Washing and dressing: explain reaching, fastening clothes, getting into or out of a bath or shower, and which help is needed, rather than only listing painful joints.
  • Moving around: describe how far you can stand and move reliably, pace, pain, rests, aids and whether you can repeat it. Do not push through pain or risk a fall to produce a distance for a claim.

Difficulties with stairs, shopping or housework can help explain daily life, but are not automatic standalone PIP points. Link evidence to the assessed activity rather than assuming every difficult chore is a descriptor.

What evidence is useful?

Use relevant clinic letters, treatment lists, occupational therapy or physiotherapy reports, care plans and your own activity examples. A diagnosis letter can confirm the condition; it may not explain the help you need. Describe actual incidents, how often they happen and what another person does. Do not invent symptoms, exaggerate or send unrelated private records simply to make the bundle larger.

The official claim page explains the current phone, post and online routes. Follow the deadline on your form and ask the PIP enquiry service for more time if needed. You may be assessed if more information is required; an assessment is not automatic in every claim. Keep copies of what you submit.

Current weekly PIP rates

Checked on 18 November 2026 against GOV.UK PIP amounts: daily living is £76.70 standard or £114.60 enhanced; mobility is £30.30 standard or £80.00 enhanced, per week. These are the current 2026 to 2027 amounts, not a forecast of your award. Check the official page again before relying on a figure.

If you disagree with the decision

For DWP PIP decisions, you usually request mandatory reconsideration within one month of the decision date. Explain which findings are wrong and why, using activity examples and evidence. Late requests may be possible with reasons; get advice promptly rather than assuming a missed month ends every option. Follow your decision letter and use the Northern Ireland service if that is where your claim is handled.

Citizens Advice's England guidance warns that challenging an existing award can put the whole award under review, so it could go down as well as up. Ask for individual advice. Scotland has a different decision-review process. Our refused-claim guide is a starting point, not a substitute for a welfare adviser or the instructions on your letter.

key_takeaways: Arthritis does not automatically qualify: PIP assesses particular daily living and mobility activities, separately.
Describe safety, acceptable standard, repeatability, time and frequency, not just one difficult or better day.
Use the correct national benefit and service; Scotland uses Adult Disability Payment for new working-age claims.
Keep deadlines in view and seek welfare advice; a challenge can put an existing award at risk.
